tagline: A prophet of the rebuilding: night visions, a call to return, and oracles of a coming king whose humility and piercing the Gospels saw fulfilled in Jesus.
overview:
Zechariah is the longest of the twelve shorter prophetic books that close the Old Testament, and many readers find it the most difficult. It opens in Jerusalem around 520 BC, less than twenty years after the first exiles came home from Babylon. The temple still lay in ruins, the returned community was small and poor, and the great promises of the earlier prophets seemed a long way off. Zechariah, working alongside the prophet Haggai, called the people to return to God and to finish rebuilding his house, and he told them what he had seen in a single night: eight visions of horses, horns, lampstands, a flying scroll, and chariots, each explained by an angel, all saying that God had not forgotten Jerusalem.

The book falls into two halves. Chapters 1 to 8 are dated to the reign of the Persian king Darius I and are full of the rebuilding: the visions, the cleansing and crowning of the high priest Joshua, words to the governor Zerubbabel, and a set of promises that turns the people's mourning fasts into feasts. Chapters 9 to 14 carry no dates and read differently. They are two collections of oracles, each headed with the word for a prophetic burden, about a king coming to Zion, shepherds good and worthless, a Jerusalem besieged and rescued, a fountain opened for cleansing, and a final day when the LORD will be king over all the earth.

The book matters to Christians out of all proportion to its size, because the Gospel writers turned to it again and again to tell the story of Jesus's last week. The king riding a donkey (9:9), the thirty pieces of silver thrown to the potter (11:12-13), the one who is pierced (12:10), and the shepherd struck so the sheep scatter (13:7) all appear in the passion narratives. Zechariah is where the New Testament learned to speak of a humble, rejected, and pierced king.
author:
The book names its prophet as Zechariah son of Berechiah, the son of Iddo (1:1). The books of Ezra call him simply the son of Iddo (Ezra 5:1; 6:14), perhaps because his grandfather was the better-known figure or because his father died young, and Nehemiah 12:16 lists a Zechariah as head of the priestly family of Iddo in the next generation. If these are the same man, Zechariah was a priest as well as a prophet, which fits his deep interest in the temple, the high priest, and purity.

That Zechariah stands behind chapters 1 to 8 is widely agreed. Chapters 9 to 14 are debated. They contain no dates, no night visions, no interpreting angel, and no mention of Zechariah, Joshua, Zerubbabel, or the temple rebuilding; they are written largely in poetry and speak of Greece (9:13), Assyria, and Egypt. Most critical scholars since the nineteenth century attribute them to one or more later, unnamed prophets (often called Second Zechariah, sometimes divided again into chapters 9 to 11 and 12 to 14), noting that the heading used at 9:1 and 12:1 also opens Malachi, so that the Twelve may end with three anonymous oracle collections. Some older scholars, prompted partly by Matthew's attribution of the thirty pieces of silver to Jeremiah, placed chapters 9 to 11 before the exile. Many conservative scholars hold that Zechariah wrote the whole book, and that the change of style reflects a different genre and a later stage of his ministry. Scholars on every side have also traced real connections between the halves: the cleansing of the land, Jerusalem's future, the shepherd-leaders, and the nations coming to worship. The book as it stands was received as one prophetic book, and it is read here that way.
date:
Chapters 1 to 8 are dated precisely by the reign of Darius I of Persia. Zechariah's first word came in the eighth month of Darius's second year, October or November of 520 BC (1:1). The night visions came on the twenty-fourth day of the eleventh month of that year, around February 519 BC (1:7). The question about fasting came in Darius's fourth year, in the ninth month, around December 518 BC (7:1). The temple was finished in Darius's sixth year, in 515 BC (Ezra 6:15).

The date of chapters 9 to 14 depends on the authorship question. Those who hold that Zechariah wrote them place them later in his own life, perhaps in the early fifth century BC, when Persia was at war with the Greek cities. Many critical scholars place them in the fifth or fourth century BC, and some later still, reading the mention of Greece and the march of chapter 9 against the conquests of Alexander the Great in 333 and 332 BC. A smaller number have argued for a date before the exile for parts of chapters 9 to 11.
setting:
In 539 BC the Persian king Cyrus took Babylon, and within a year he allowed exiled Judeans to return and rebuild the temple in Jerusalem (Ezra 1). The returned community set up the altar and laid the temple's foundations, but opposition from neighbors and their own discouragement stopped the work for about sixteen years (Ezra 3 and 4). When Darius I seized the Persian throne in 522 BC, revolts broke out across the empire before he secured his rule. In 520 BC, in the second year of his reign, Haggai and then Zechariah urged the people to start building again (Ezra 5:1-2). Judah was then a small province of the Persian Empire, governed by Zerubbabel, a grandson of King Jehoiachin, with Joshua son of Jehozadak as high priest.

The first readers were a disappointed people. The land was poor and the harvests thin. Jerusalem had few inhabitants and broken walls. The throne of David was empty, and the prophets had promised far more than this. The new temple looked like nothing beside the memory of Solomon's (Haggai 2:3). Zechariah speaks into that gap between promise and experience.
purpose: Zechariah wrote to call a discouraged community back to God and to the work in front of them. The book opens with a summons, return to me and I will return to you (1:3), and a warning not to repeat the fathers' refusal to listen. The visions assure the people that God rules the nations, that he is jealous for Jerusalem, that he will cleanse his people's guilt, and that the temple will be finished by his Spirit rather than by force. Chapters 7 and 8 insist that fasting means nothing without justice and mercy toward the widow, the orphan, the stranger, and the poor. Chapters 9 to 14 lift the reader's eyes further, to a future in which God will send a king, judge the false shepherds, cleanse his people through grief and a fountain of cleansing, and gather the nations to worship him in a holy Jerusalem. The book was written for people who had come home and still waited for the fullness of what home was supposed to be.
story: Zechariah stands near the end of the Old Testament story. Before him lie the fall of Jerusalem in 587 or 586 BC, the exile in Babylon, and the return under Cyrus told in Ezra 1 to 3. His ministry overlaps Haggai's and belongs to the same moment as Ezra 5 and 6, when the second temple was built. After him come the work of Ezra and Nehemiah in the fifth century BC and the last of the prophets, Malachi. Then the Old Testament falls silent for about four centuries, and the next time these streets appear in Scripture, a king rides into Jerusalem on a donkey while the crowd sings.
christ: Few Old Testament books are drawn on more heavily in the Gospels' account of Jesus's last days. Matthew and John both say that Jesus's entry into Jerusalem on a donkey fulfilled Zechariah 9:9 (Matthew 21:4-5; John 12:14-15). Jesus himself cited Zechariah 13:7 on the night of his arrest, the shepherd struck and the sheep scattered (Matthew 26:31; Mark 14:27). Matthew connects the thirty pieces of silver paid to Judas, returned to the temple and used to buy a potter's field, with Zechariah 11:12-13, though he credits the words to Jeremiah (Matthew 27:3-10). John sees Zechariah 12:10 fulfilled when a soldier pierced Jesus's side (John 19:37), and Revelation 1:7 applies the same verse to his return. The Branch who will build the temple and be a priest on his throne (3:8; 6:12-13), the fountain opened for sin and uncleanness (13:1), and the living waters flowing from Jerusalem (14:8) have all been read as pointing to Christ, while Revelation draws on Zechariah's horses, lampstands, and olive trees (Revelation 6; 11:4). Taken together, the book gives the New Testament its picture of a king who comes in humility, is valued at a slave's price, is pierced by his own people, and yet reigns over all the earth.
reading:
Read chapters 1 to 6 as apocalyptic vision: symbolic scenes interpreted by an angel, closer to a dream than to a report. Don't press every detail for a hidden meaning; ask what the angel says the vision means, and let that carry the weight. The visions move in a pattern, beginning and ending with horses patrolling the earth, with the visions of the high priest and the lampstand at the center. Read chapters 7 and 8 as prophetic sermons, and chapters 9 to 14 as poetic oracles about the future, full of older prophetic language from Isaiah, Jeremiah, and Ezekiel.

Two cautions help. First, the later chapters are highly figurative. Readers disagree whether their battles and blessings refer to events after the exile, to the coming of Christ and the church, to a future restoration of Israel, or to several of these, and it's wise to hold detailed timetables loosely. Second, the text of Zechariah is difficult in places, and translations differ; where a note says the Hebrew is uncertain, it is. The steady line through all of it is simple: the LORD has returned to his people, he will cleanse them, and he will be king over all the earth.

structure.title: A call to return
structure.summary: Zechariah's first message, in late 520 BC, calls the people to return to the LORD and not to repeat their fathers' refusal to listen to the prophets.

structure.title: Eight night visions and a crowning
structure.summary: In one night Zechariah sees eight visions, from the horsemen among the myrtles to the four chariots, each interpreted by an angel. They promise God's return to Jerusalem, judgment on the nations, the cleansing of the high priest and the land, and the completion of the temple, and they close with a symbolic crown and a word about the Branch.

structure.title: Fasts turned to feasts
structure.summary: A question about fasting, in 518 BC, prompts a call to justice and mercy, a reminder of why the exile came, and ten promises of a restored Jerusalem to which the nations will come seeking God.

structure.title: The first burden: the coming king and the rejected shepherd
structure.summary: God marches against Israel's neighbors, a humble king rides into Zion, the scattered people are gathered, and a prophetic shepherd is rejected and valued at thirty pieces of silver.

structure.title: The second burden: Jerusalem cleansed and the LORD as king
structure.summary: Jerusalem is besieged and rescued, the people mourn for the one they have pierced, a fountain is opened to cleanse them, the shepherd is struck, and the LORD becomes king over all the earth.

themes.title: Return
themes.body: The book opens with God's invitation, return to me and I will return to you (1:3), and the whole of it unfolds that promise. The people are to turn from the ways of their fathers; God, in turn, comes back to Jerusalem with mercy, to live among them. Zechariah insists that the exile was real judgment for real refusal (7:11-14), and that God's return is pure mercy rather than a reward earned.

themes.title: Cleansing
themes.body: Zechariah's concern is not only a rebuilt building but a purified people. The high priest's filthy garments are removed (chapter 3), wickedness is carried away to Babylon in a basket (chapter 5), a fountain is opened for sin and impurity (13:1), and at the end even the cooking pots of Jerusalem are holy (14:20-21). God does not simply return to the people as they are; he makes them fit for his presence.

themes.title: Temple and leadership
themes.body: The first half turns on the rebuilding of the temple and on the two leaders of the community, Joshua the high priest and Zerubbabel the governor from David's line. The Branch will build the temple and bear royal splendor (6:12-13), and the work will succeed by God's Spirit rather than by military power (4:6). The second half turns to shepherds: faithless leaders who fleece the flock, and a shepherd whom the people reject.

themes.title: The king who comes humbly
themes.body: Zechariah's king comes riding a donkey, righteous and humble (9:9), and he speaks peace to the nations. The same half of the book speaks of a shepherd valued at thirty pieces of silver and of one who is pierced and mourned. The book holds together royal victory and suffering rejection in a way that puzzled its readers until the Gospels read both in the life of one man.

themes.title: The nations and the kingdom of God
themes.body: The nations who scattered Judah will be judged (1:18-21), but many nations will also join themselves to the LORD (2:11), ten men will grasp the robe of a Jew to go with him to God (8:23), and survivors of the nations will come up each year to worship the King (14:16). The book ends with the LORD as king over all the earth and holiness spread into every corner of ordinary life.

keyChapters.why: The call to return and the first night vision, in which God declares that he is jealous for Jerusalem and will return to it with mercy.
Joshua the high priest, accused by Satan, is stripped of filthy garments and clothed in clean ones, a picture of forgiveness, and the promised Branch is announced.
The golden lampstand and the two olive trees, with the book's best-known word: not by might nor by power, but by God's Spirit.
Ten promises of a restored Jerusalem, where old people sit in the streets, children play, fasts become feasts, and the nations come seeking God.
The king who comes to Zion humble and riding on a donkey, the text the Gospels quote at Jesus's entry into Jerusalem.
The shepherd who is rejected and paid thirty pieces of silver, which Matthew connects with Judas's betrayal.
The spirit of grace poured out and the people's mourning for the one they have pierced, cited by John at the cross.
The day of the LORD, living waters flowing from Jerusalem, and the LORD as king over all the earth.
